title: Resource Rankings
text:
The Lake Rankings provide anglers with a simple way to compare Alabama’s public fisheries based on the qualities that matter most on the water. Rather than relying on a single measurement, each lake is evaluated using information collected during standardized electrofishing fisheries surveys. These measurements are converted into standardized scores so they can be compared fairly across lakes, then combined into rankings based on different angler preferences. Whether your goal is to catch lots of fish, target trophy-sized fish, or find a balance between the two, the rankings can help identify lakes that best match your fishing preference. To provide an up-to-date picture of each fishery, rankings are based on the most recent year of data available rather than calculating an average across sampling years. Although fishing success can vary with weather, season, and other environmental conditions, these rankings offer a consistent, science-based comparison of Alabama’s fisheries using sampling events from long-term monitoring data collected by ADCNR biologists.
Fish Size Groups Stock size fish are 5 inches for crappie, 7 inches for spotted bass/Alabama bass, and 8 inches for largemouth bass. Preferred size fish are 10 inches for crappie, 14 inches for spotted bass/Alabama bass, and 15 inches for largemouth bass. Memorable size fish are 12 inches for crappie, 17 inches for spotted bass/Alabama bass, and 20 inches for largemouth bass.
Catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) measures the number of fish caught for a given amount of sampling effort, such as fish collected per hour of electrofishing. CPUE helps biologists track changes in relative abundance over time and determine whether fish populations are increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable.
Age at Length (TTR) is the time-to-reach preferred size for each species.
*Please contact the district biologist with any data or resource specific questions (link below).

title: ADCNR, Freshwater Fisheries Division
text:
Freshwater Fisheries Division










Alabama is home to a rich network of rivers and reservoirs that support thriving fisheries and some of the most diverse aquatic ecosystems in the country. Anglers can find ample opportunities for bass, crappie, catfish, and other popular sport fish in the flowing waters of the Alabama and Tombigbee Rivers, large impoundments like Guntersville Reservoir, and coastal systems such as the expansive Mobile-Tensaw River Delta. Sampling and data collection are central to maintaining healthy fish populations for both conservation and recreation, and fisheries biologists regularly monitor these populations to ensure Alabama’s fisheries remain abundant, balanced, and enjoyable for anglers of all skill levels.

Boat Ramps and Access: Outdoor Alabama Freshwater Boating Access

title: Introduction
text:
The information below highlights some of the surveys and key metrics used by Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (ADCNR) Freshwater Fisheries biologists to monitor fish populations and guide management decisions. These measurements help biologists evaluate fish abundance, growth, size structure, and overall health. Brief explanations of several commonly used metrics are provided below. For additional information, please contact your local district biologist.
Catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) measures the number of fish caught for a given amount of sampling effort, such as fish collected per hour of electrofishing. CPUE helps biologists track changes in relative abundance over time and determine whether fish populations are increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable.
Relative Weight (Wr) compares a fish’s weight to the expected weight for a fish of the same length. This metric provides an indication of overall health and body condition. Fish with higher relative weights are generally considered healthier, and values can exceed 100, but 100 is considered excellent condition.
Age at Length (TTR) estimates the average amount of time required for a fish to grow to a specific size. This information helps biologists assess growth rates and evaluate the quality of a fishery.
Together, these metrics provide valuable insight into fish population health, growth, and the overall quality of Alabama’s fisheries.
*Empty figures indicate a lack of data or insufficient data to produce the figure.
*Fishery data exists for resources not listed here. Please contact district staff for more information (see link below).

title: Introduction
text:
Mobile-Tensaw River Delta
The Mobile–Tensaw River Delta, one of the largest and most ecologically diverse river deltas in the United States, encompasses more than 250,000 acres of rivers, swamps, marshes, and floodplain forests in coastal Alabama. Formed by the confluence of the Mobile, Tensaw, and Apalachee rivers, the delta is renowned as a premier freshwater fishing and wildlife system in the Southeast. Managed cooperatively by state and federal partners, with hydrology driven by natural river flows and upstream water control projects, the delta supports extensive aquatic habitat and productivity. These diverse environments sustain abundant fisheries, including largemouth bass, crappie spp., sunfish, striped bass, catfish, and a wide array of estuarine and migratory species.

Location: Southwest Alabama, north of Mobile Bay
Size: 20,323 acres
Max Depth: 100 feet
Impounded: Free flowing from Claiborne and Coffeeville dams

title: Introduction
text:
Coffeeville Reservoir
Coffeeville Reservoir, a run-of-the-river impoundment on the Tombigbee River in southwest Alabama, extends approximately 97 river miles from Coffeeville Lock and Dam upstream to Demopolis Lock and Dam. Operated by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the reservoir functions primarily as a navigation corridor while maintaining riverine characteristics and seasonal flow variability. This system supports a diverse assemblage of aquatic habitats, including main-channel, backwater, and floodplain environments. As a result, Coffeeville Reservoir sustains productive fisheries for largemouth bass, crappie spp., bream, and catfish.

Location: Southwest Alabama, between Coffeeville and Demopolis Lock and Dam
Size: 8,500 acres
Max Depth: 40 ft.
Impounded: 1960, (Old Lock One dates back to 1915)

Bankhead Reservoir
Bankhead Dam impounds the three main forks of the Black Warrior River, creating a 9,200 acre reservoir with 172 miles of boatable tributaries and backwaters for anglers to explore. The lake supports a trophy striped bass fishery and abundant populations of largemouth bass, Alabama bass, crappie, sunfish, and catfish. Access to the reservoir is mostly by private pay launches. However, ADCNR provides three boating access areas to the upper Mulberry Fork.

Claiborne Reservoir

It was the last impoundment constructed on the Alabama River by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in 1970. Claiborne provides excellent fishing for largemouth bass, crappie and catfish. Lake Eufaula

The minimally developed northern section of Lake Eufaula falls within the 11,160-acre Eufaula National Wildlife Refuge. The lake supports abundant gamefish such as largemouth bass, black crappie, bream, and catfish.

Holt Reservoir

The United States Army Corps of Engineers oversees navigation, flood control, and reservoir operations. Boaters are required to purchase a day use pass or an annual pass from USACE to access the reservoir. In addition to excellent fishing for Alabama bass and blue catfish, the lake also supports an abundance of other species such as largemouth bass, crappie, bream, channel catfish, flathead catfish, skipjack herring, and paddlefish.

It is best known for its deep clear water and excellent fishing opportunities for Alabama bass, largemouth bass, striped bass, and crappie. Birmingham Water Works oversees flood control and reservoir operations. There are two boat ramps available for a $5.00 fee. However, the ramp at the upper end of the lake is closed during winter drawdowns. Contact Birmingham Water Works with any questions regarding boat ramp access.

Lake Guntersville is operated by the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), whose operations preserve critical aquatic habitats through water-level control and invasive plant management. The lake supports abundant gamefish such as largemouth bass, spotted bass, smallmouth bass, both black and white crappie, bream (primarily bluegill and redear sunfish), sauger, white bass, striped bass, and trophy-sized catfish (channel, blue, and flathead).

Wheeler Reservoir
Wheeler Reservoir (aka Wheeler Lake) is Alabama’s second largest reservoir and encompasses roughly 67,070 acres and 1,027 miles of shoreline. It is known for the bass fishing area called the “Decatur Flats”, a large backwater area on the north side of the river channel with aquatic vegetation, stump rows, and several creek channels. These operations preserve critical aquatic habitats through water-level control. The lake supports abundant gamefish such as largemouth bass, spotted bass, smallmouth bass, crappie, bream, sauger, white bass, striped bass, and trophy-sized blue catfish.

Lay Lake is in central Alabama and was the first hydropower facility constructed by Alabama Power on the Coosa River system. Alabama Power oversees reservoir operations on this 12,000-acre impoundment. Lay Lake is one of the state’s premier fisheries for both Alabama bass and largemouth bass. Annual striped bass stockings create bank or boat angling opportunities in the Logan Martin tailrace during early spring. Lay also has abundant populations of crappie, catfish, and bream.

Location: Central Alabama – near Clanton, Shelby, Columbiana, Vincent, Childersburg
Size: 12,000 acres
Max Depth: 88 feet
Impounded: 1914

Logan Martin Lake
Logan Martin Reservoir is a 15,000-acre impoundment of the Coosa River in east central Alabama. Its proximity to the city of Birmingham and location adjacent to I-20 has made it a popular destination for boaters and anglers alike. Alabama Power oversees reservoir and hydropower operations. The lake supports healthy populations of largemouth bass and the hard-fighting Alabama bass. Striped bass are a popular target among anglers fishing the tailrace below Neely Henry Dam, as fish congregate in the upper reaches of the reservoir in the early spring. The lake also supports abundant populations of crappie, catfish, and bluegill.

Location: Central/Northeast Alabama – near Lincoln, Pell City, Riverside, and Ohatchee
Size: 15,263 acres
Max Depth: 80 feet

Lake Mitchell
Mitchell Reservoir is the smallest impoundment on the Coosa River and the second completed by Alabama Power on the Coosa River system. Mitchell Reservoir offers stunning scenery due to its largely undeveloped shoreline, and natural islands located in the headwaters below Lay Dam. Alabama Power oversees hydroelectric operations, navigation, flood control, and reservoir operations. Both largemouth bass and Alabama bass are abundant, and hybrid striped bass stockings create bank and boat fishing opportunities. The lake also supports populations of crappie, catfish species, and bream.

Neely Henry Reservoir
Neely Henry Reservoir is an 11,200-acre impoundment on the Coosa River in northeast Alabama. Alabama Power oversees reservoir operations at this hydropower facility. The lake supports healthy populations of largemouth bass, the hard-fighting Alabama bass and abundant fisheries for catfish and bream. Crappie fishing at Neely Henry goes under the radar but can be fantastic in the spring.

Smith Lake
Lewis Smith Lake is a tributary storage impoundment of the Sipsey Fork of the Black Warrior River. It is an expansive reservoir with over 500 miles of shoreline. Alabama Power Company oversees flood control and reservoir operations. It is best known for its deep clear water and excellent fishing opportunities for striped bass, Alabama bass, and crappie.

title: Introduction
text:
Weiss Lake
Weiss Reservoir (pronounced ‘Wice’) spans 30,000 acres in northeast Alabama near the Alabama-Georgia border. Alabama Power oversees reservoir operations at this hydropower impoundment. Weiss has historically been known as one of the state’s premier crappie fisheries, attracting numerous non-resident anglers annually to harvest large black and white crappie. The lake also supports healthy bass fisheries for largemouth bass and Alabama bass. Blue catfish, channel catfish, and flathead catfish are also popular target species among anglers and can reach trophy size, while bream fishing at Weiss can be great in the summertime, particularly when insects such as mayflies are hatching.

Location: Northeast Alabama – near Leesburg, Cedar Bluff, Centre and Gaylesville
Size: 30,027 acres
Max Depth: 62 feet
Impounded: 1961

Little Bear Creek Reservoir
Little Bear Creek Reservoir is one of four lakes constructed by the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) as part of the Bear Creek Waterway Control Project to control floodwater. The surrounding land is managed by the Bear Creek Development Authority (BCDA). A user’s permit is required for those between the ages of 16 and 65. The lake supports abundant gamefish such as largemouth bass, spotted bass, crappie, bream, and catfish. Forage species such as threadfin shad and gizzard shad help sustain sportfish within the reservoir.

Location: Northwest Alabama about 13 miles west of Russellville
Size: 1,560 acres
Max Depth: 84 feet
Impounded: 1976

Lake Martin is the largest impoundment on the Tallapoosa River with over 780 miles of shoreline. Alabama Power Company oversees flood control and reservoir operations. Demopolis Reservoir
Demopolis Reservoir is a mainstem impoundment of the Tombigbee River with ample backwater habitat. It is operated by the United States Army Corps of Engineers. Operations provide anglers boating access, bank fishing access, and invasive plant management. Boaters are required to purchase a day use pass or an annual pass from USACE to access the reservoir. The lake supports abundant gamefish populations such as largemouth bass, crappie, bream, and catfish.

title: Introduction

Jones Bluff Reservoir
Jones Bluff Reservoir is the first reservoir on the Alabama River, just below the confluence of the Tallapoosa River and Coosa River. It is a run of the river reservoir with a few creeks and back water areas that can flood during heavy rainfall. These backwater areas are popular for bass and crappie anglers, especially in the spring. Most of the shoreline of Jones Bluff Reservoir is undeveloped and offers an abundance of aquatic vegetation, stumps, and blowdowns to target fish. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers oversees all reservoir operations. Jones Bluff is best known for fantastic crappie fishing, as well as black bass and catfish species.

Thurlow Reservoir
Thurlow Reservoir is the smallest reservoir on the Tallapoosa River, located just below Yates Reservoir. Most of the shoreline of Thurlow Reservoir is undeveloped, offering steep, rocky habitat as well as the occasional blowdown to hold fish. Alabama Power Co. oversees hydroelectric operations, navigation, flood control, and reservoir operations. It is an underutilized lake with good populations of most sport fish species.

title: Introduction
text:
Yates Lake
Yates Reservoir is a small reservoir located immediately below Lake Martin Dam on the Tallapoosa River. The reservoir often has cooler water in the summer compared to other reservoirs as water flows in from a deep discharge on Martin Dam. Much of the shoreline of Yates Reservoir is undeveloped, offering steep, rocky habitat as well as the occasional blowdown to hold fish. In recent years, submersed aquatic vegetation has become established, particularly in the upper reaches near Martin Dam as well as the backs of coves. Alabama Power Co. oversees hydroelectric operations, navigation, flood control, and reservoir operations. It is an often underutilized lake with healthy populations of striped bass, largemouth bass, Alabama bass, yellow perch, and crappie (both black and white).

Location: East-central Alabama – near Tallassee
Size: 1,980 acres
Max Depth: 60 feet
Impounded: 1928
